reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: An adrenal incidentaloma is an adrenal mass discovered unexpectedly on imaging performed for an unrelated reason, and its evaluation centres on two questions: is it functional, and is it malignant
Every incidentaloma should be screened biochemically for cortisol excess, phaeochromocytoma, and, in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients, primary aldosteronism
Unenhanced CT attenuation is key: a lipid-rich lesion with low Hounsfield values strongly favours a benign adenoma, while high attenuation warrants further characterisation
Large size and imaging features such as irregular margins, heterogeneity, and delayed contrast washout raise concern for adrenocortical carcinoma
Phaeochromocytoma must be excluded before any biopsy or surgery to avoid a catastrophic hypertensive crisis

Surgery (usually laparoscopic adrenalectomy) is indicated for functional tumours, lesions with malignant features, and masses above a threshold size, while smaller non-functioning benign lesions are monitored
Biopsy of an adrenal mass is rarely helpful and is reserved for suspected metastasis or infiltrative disease after phaeochromocytoma has been ruled out
reference.pathophysiology: Adrenal incidentalomas are a heterogeneous group. Most are benign non-functioning cortical adenomas, but the differential spans hormonally active adenomas (secreting cortisol or aldosterone), phaeochromocytomas arising from the adrenal medulla, adrenocortical carcinoma, myelolipomas, cysts, and metastatic deposits. Functional lesions cause disease through autonomous hormone secretion: cortisol excess produces subclinical or overt Cushing syndrome, aldosterone excess produces hypertension and hypokalaemia, and catecholamine excess from a phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension and its complications. Malignant potential correlates with size, growth rate, and imaging characteristics reflecting lipid content and vascularity.
additionalDifferentials: Adrenal metastasis or myelolipoma or adrenal cyst
additionalInvestigations: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (and where indicated late-night salivary or 24-hour urinary cortisol) for autonomous cortisol secretion
Plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma
Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients
Unenhanced CT for attenuation, with contrast washout study or MRI chemical-shift imaging to characterise indeterminate lesions
Serial imaging surveillance for non-operated lesions to assess growth
Consideration of adrenal vein sampling when lateralising aldosterone excess before surgery
redFlags: Undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma before intervention, risking a life-threatening hypertensive crisis on biopsy or induction
Large or rapidly enlarging mass with heterogeneous, high-attenuation, poorly washing-out features suggesting adrenocortical carcinoma
Severe or resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia indicating a functioning tumour
Known extra-adrenal malignancy with a new adrenal lesion suggesting metastasis
reference.prognosis: Most incidentalomas are benign and non-functioning with an excellent outlook and stable behaviour on surveillance. Functional lesions generally do well after adrenalectomy with resolution or improvement of hormone excess, whereas adrenocortical carcinoma carries a poor prognosis, strongly influenced by stage and completeness of resection.
pitfalls: Proceeding to biopsy or surgery without first excluding a phaeochromocytoma
Labelling a mass non-functioning without complete biochemical screening, missing subclinical cortisol excess
Underestimating malignant potential by relying on size alone and ignoring washout and morphology
Inadequate perioperative alpha- (then beta-) blockade when operating on a catecholamine-secreting tumour
Failing to plan perioperative glucocorticoid cover when removing a cortisol-secreting adenoma with a suppressed contralateral gland
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Screen every incidentaloma biochemically for autonomous cortisol secretion, phaeochromocytoma, and primary aldosteronism in hypertensive or hypokalaemic patients
Characterise the lesion with unenhanced CT attenuation, using contrast washout or chemical-shift MRI for indeterminate masses
Exclude and, where present, medically prepare a phaeochromocytoma with alpha-blockade before any biopsy or surgery
Refer for adrenalectomy, usually laparoscopic, for functional tumours, imaging features suspicious for malignancy, or masses above a threshold size
Undertake adrenal vein sampling to lateralise aldosterone excess before surgery when indicated
Monitor non-operated benign non-functioning lesions with interval imaging and biochemical review
Coordinate assessment through endocrinology and endocrine surgery
